title: What exactly is a "petard"? | FOSSIL WORDS

entries.note: A word that survives mainly inside one phrase or idiom, a leftover trace of older usage, like [[see:fro]] in to and fro.
Old English preposition and adverb meaning away or backwards, akin to from, now surviving only in to and fro.
Old description of someone who always does the opposite of what is wanted; a difficult, contrary person.
New technology keeping design elements of older technology, like a phone's shutter sound; Jess calls fossil words a lexical version of it.
Its pod comes from [[from:iPod]]s, the only devices that could first play them, and may become a fossil element.
The device that gave the pod in [[gave:podcast]], likely to be used only for the old technology in future.
Unpaired words, discussed in an earlier episode.
From Latin [[from:clemens]], placid or mild, so inclement weather is not mild; shares its origin with [[same-root:clemency]].
Meaning mercy, still in use and sharing its origin with [[same-root:inclement]].
Survives only in ulterior motives; built on [[from:ultra]], beyond, meaning further away than [[see:exterior]].
In here, contrasted with [[see:exterior]] and [[see:ulterior]], which was once just as common.
Out there, contrasted with [[see:ulterior]], which is even further beyond.
Not from out and rage but from Latin [[from:ultra]] via French, meaning extraness, so outrageous fashion is out there rather than enraging.
Shrift was confession or absolution; short shrift was the brief chance to confess given to the condemned, quoted from Scott's Quentin Durward.
American crime slang for on the run; Elizabethan lam meant to beat, so possibly like [[see:beat it]], and maybe related to [[same-root?:lambast]].
Offered as a playful synonym for getting out quickly, as in [[see:on the lam]].
Compared with [[see:on the lam]], which may imply the same idea of leaving fast.
Originally pronounced lambaste, a repetitive compound of lam and bast, both meaning beat; now means verbal attack; unrelated to [[unrelated:baste]].
Putting liquid on food, unrelated to the bast in [[unrelated:lambast]].
Boodle, from Dutch [[from:boedel]], property, plus a playful c; kit may be a wooden vessel, so the whole ship and cargo; a born fossil.
Thieves' slang phrase containing the same boodle as [[see:kit and caboodle]].
A word that has only ever existed in one fixed context, like caboodle in [[see:kit and caboodle]].
A modern born fossil: nother appears only here, a modern example of [[see:rebracketing]].
Word-boundary shifts behind [[see:a whole nother]], [[see:nickname]], [[see:run amok]] and [[see:tarnation]]; also the topic of an earlier episode.
From would rathers, as in to have one's druthers, common in the American South; a born fossil.
A knell is a slow mournful bell tolled when someone died or at funerals; also called the [[see:passing bell]] or death bell.
Another name, alongside death bell, for the bell rung at a death, as in [[see:death knell]].

entries.term: the final nail in the coffin
entries.note: An idiom with the same meaning as sounding the [[equivalent:death knell]].

entries.term: the straw that breaks the camel's back
entries.note: An alternative idiom offered for [[equivalent:death knell]].
Edgar Allan Poe's poem, where knell appears unfossilized as a verb, which Jess cites against [[see:death knell]].
Mostly in living vicariously but spreading; meaning taking another's place, first used of Jesus dying for humanity; related to [[same-root:vicar]].
Psychology concept where Rob first met [[see:vicarious]].
Related to [[same-root:vicarious]] as someone who stands as a representative.
Means shape, so a figment of your imagination is a shape it takes; sometimes eggcorned as [[see:pigment of the imagination]].
An [[see:eggcorn]] of figment of the imagination.
Fossil words invite eggcorns, since people replace unfamiliar words with ones they know.
Deserts is a nounification of [[from:deserve]], what you deserve, with one s; discussed in earlier episodes.
Survives in champing at the bit, a horse chewing its bit; an alternative to [[same-root:chomping]], quoted from Smollett and The Hobbit.
Chomping at the bit isn't so wrong, as [[see:champing]] is really just an alternative form.
Related to [[same-root:abate]]; often eggcorned as fishing [[see:bait]], which is understandable.
The word related to bated in [[see:bated breath]].
Fishing bait, the source of the eggcorned spelling of [[see:bated breath]].
Bide, from an older English word meaning to stay or continue, is fossilized here, though [[same-root:abide]] survives.
Related to bide in [[same-root:bide your time]]; meaning to stay, as in [[see:Abide with Me]] and the Dude abides.
Coen Brothers film whose line the Dude abides Jess cites for [[see:abide]].
Hymn whose title Rob realises essentially means stay with me, via [[see:abide]].
Eke meant to increase or lengthen, so to eke out is to stretch something; related to [[same-root:nickname]].
Originally an ekename, an additional name, rebracketed; related to [[same-root:eke out]].
Beck is a variant of [[same-root:beckon]], a silent commanding gesture; beck is typically the noun, beckon the verb.
A silent gesture indicating a command, like a curled finger; essentially the same word as beck in [[same-root:beck and call]].
Kith also meant your people, so a near reduplication; Rob reads it as friends and family, like [[equivalent:friends and family]].
The alliterative phrase that makes [[equivalent:kith and kin]] unnecessary.
From Portuguese accounts using amouco, from a Malay word meaning attack furiously; later a culture-bound syndrome; problematic; amuck spelling from [[see:muck]].
Conflated with amok, giving the spelling amuck and the rebracketed run a muck in [[see:run amok]].
Stereotypical Texan oath used by [[see:Yosemite Sam]], rebracketed from by the eternal via [[from:tarnal]], influenced by [[see:darnation]]; a born fossil.
Looney Tunes character Jess associates with what in [[see:tarnation]], letting him swear on children's TV.
Shortening of eternal, the step leading to [[gave:tarnation]].
Minced oath softening damnation that probably influenced [[see:tarnation]].
From Hamlet's hoist with his own petard, about turning the tables on assassins: blown up by your own bomb.
A small siege bomb for blowing in doors; French pétard is still a banger, sharing a root with [[same-root:péter]], to fart.
French to fart, sharing its root with [[same-root:petard]], so hoisted by your own fart bomb.
French verb for firing a volley of gunshots, which can also mean emitting a stream of farts.
Shebang, of unknown origin, meant a shelter in Walt Whitman, a tavern, or a Yale dorm, so the whole place; maybe related to [[same-root?:shebeen]].
Irish word, also used in South Africa, for an informal or illicit bar; possibly related to [[same-root?:the whole shebang]].
Fettle, a Lancashire dialect word for condition, probably from an Old English word for a girdle or belt.
Hale means healthy and uninjured, perhaps a Scots version of [[from?:whole]].
In Old English also meant free from injury, perhaps the source of hale in [[gave?:hale and hearty]].
The verb corresponding to the noun [[same-root:heist]].
Noun matching the verb [[same-root:hoist]], literally a lifting, like lifting something off someone.
A batten is a wooden bar holding down a door or hatch; spelled differently from [[same-root?:baton]], possibly the same word.
Compared with batten in [[see:batten down the hatches]]; perhaps a French versus English spelling of one word.
Lo, a verb form of the Old English word for look, was an all-purpose exclamation for surprise, greeting, joy or grief.
From Latin [[from:turpis]], vile, foul or ugly, so literally utter depravity.
Spick was a nail and span a wood chip, both freshly made, Germanic and probably Old Norse; a double fossil; compare [[see:span-new]].
16th–17th century phrase meaning [[equivalent:brand new]], showing span from [[see:spick and span]].
Same idea as [[equivalent:span-new]]: fresh from a hot branding iron.
Literally means of years, from an Old English word for formerly or in former times.
The offing just means the near future, despite sounding like murder.
